Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
The hurricane came through in the early hours of a Tuesday morning, and for Mai, the world has not felt solid since. She was fifty years old then, working the closing shift at a fast-food restaurant off the interstate in Biloxi, Mississippi. When the power cut and the sirens began, she and two younger coworkers retreated to the walk-in freezer, the only room without windows. They stayed there for seven hours, huddled among boxes of frozen fries and chicken patties, listening to the roof tear away in sheets. Mai remembers the cold, the way her fingers went numb against the metal shelving, and the sound—a constant, grinding roar that seemed to come from inside her own skull. But what she remembers most clearly are the gaps. She cannot recall how they got out. She cannot recall the drive to the shelter or the face of the man who handed her a blanket. What she has instead are fragments: the taste of metal in her mouth, the sight of a single white sneaker floating in brown water, the feeling of someone’s elbow pressing into her ribs. These pieces do not connect, and when they surface—always without warning, always when she is least prepared—they arrive with such force that Mai has to stop whatever she is doing. She will be standing at the fry station, the oil hissing, and suddenly she is back in that cold dark, and the emotion hits her chest like a physical blow. She has to brace herself against the counter, breathing hard, until the manager touches her shoulder and she snaps back.

It has been two years, and Mai has come to believe that the person she was before the storm is gone forever. She says she will never feel normal emotions again, and by this she means the quiet ones—the contentment of a slow afternoon, the mild irritation of a long line at the grocery store, the simple pleasure of watching her husband tend the garden. What she feels now is a constant, low-level dread, punctuated by spikes of terror. She has also become certain that she no longer belongs anywhere. Not in her own home, not at work, not among the people who knew her before. She looks at her coworkers laughing in the break room and feels as though she is watching them through a pane of glass. She cannot explain it, but she knows, with a certainty that feels like fact, that she has been set apart.

The effects of this are concrete and visible. Mai used to sleep beside her husband, but now she cannot. Night has become a problem. She lies awake for hours, listening to the creak of the house, the distant bark of a dog, the hum of the refrigerator. Every unexpected sound—a car door slamming, a child shouting in the street—makes her flinch and go rigid. At night, these sounds feel worse. The darkness itself feels dangerous. She has started sleeping on the couch in the living room, with every light on, the television playing a cooking show at low volume, because silence is worse. Her husband has stopped asking when she will come back to bed. He sleeps alone now, and Mai knows he is hurt, but she cannot explain to him why the bed feels like a trap, why the dark feels like a lid closing.

At work, she has become hypervigilant. The restaurant is loud—the beep of the fry timer, the slam of the freezer door, the sudden clatter of a dropped tray. Each of these sounds makes Mai’s heart race. She has started wearing earplugs under her hairnet, which her manager has noticed and warned her about because she cannot hear the drive-thru orders. She has been written up twice. What frightens her most is the feeling that she cannot stop bad things from happening. She used to believe she had some control—that if she was careful, if she planned, she could keep herself and her family safe. That belief is gone. The storm proved that safety is an illusion, and now every loud noise, every dark room, every unexpected shift in the air feels like the beginning of the next disaster.

Mai came to therapy at her husband’s insistence, but also because she is exhausted. She is tired of being afraid, tired of sleeping on the couch, tired of the way her body braces for impact even when nothing is happening. She is afraid that this is all she will ever feel. What she hopes, though she cannot quite say it out loud, is that someone will tell her how to find her way back to the person she used to be—or, if that is impossible, how to live with the person she has become.
